title: Flush Draw Facing A Small Bet
question: Should hero call, fold, or raise?
facingAction: The button bets 25 into a pot of 120.

opponentRange.notation: KK, 77, 33, 22, AK, KQ, KJs, QQ, JJ, TT, 99, A5s, 65s
opponentRange.label: a wide turn barrelling range: sets, top pair, the underpairs that missed this board, and a couple of hands with nothing

assumptions: The button bets this turn with the range stated. If this opponent only makes a small bet with hands that already beat a pair of queens, the equity figure falls and so does the case for calling.
The price comparison assumes the hand reaches showdown with no further betting after the river card. Any river bet is a separate decision at a separate price.
Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street; nobody is close to all in.
Only one card is left to come, so the two-cards-to-come version of the rule of 2 and 4 does not apply here.
reasoning: Read the board first: king high, no pair, two hearts, and two low cards — so a straight is available only to a hand holding low cards of its own, and only if the right river card arrives. You hold two more hearts, so a fifth heart on the river makes you a flush. Notice which flush: the king of hearts is on the board, so an opponent holding the ace of hearts would make a better one — this is not the nut draw, and that matters more in other spots than it does at this price. The bet is small next to the pot, which is the whole story: a small bet asks you to be best only a small share of the time, and a one-card draw of this shape gets there well under half the time but comfortably more often than a price this cheap demands. You also pick up equity you did not pay for, because against the range assumed here a queen or a jack on the river beats the underpairs it does not itself pair, and the hands with nothing. It does not beat 77, 33 or 22, which are sets on this board rather than small pairs. Both of those push the same way, so calling follows from the price rather than from any strength in your hand. Raising is a different plan with a different justification — it needs the opponent to fold hands that beat you — and nothing in this range assumption supports it. Change the price and the answer changes, which is exactly what the companion scenario does. Change the range to one containing nothing you can beat by pairing and your equity drops back to the bare draw, which is still enough here, but only just.
commonMistakes: Folding a draw because 'it probably will not get there'. How often it gets there is only half the comparison; the other half is what you are being asked to pay.
Counting the hearts and stopping, when against this range a queen or a jack also wins a share of the pots where no heart arrives.
Treating this as the nut flush draw. With the king of hearts on the board, a hand holding the ace of hearts makes a better flush than yours.
Calling here and then automatically calling a large river bet as well, as though the cheap price carried over to the next street.

title: Same Flush Draw, Huge Overbet
question: Should hero call or fold?
facingAction: The button bets 240 into a pot of 120.

opponentRange.notation: KK, 77, 33, 22, AK, KQ, KJs, QQ, JJ, TT, 99, A5s, 65s
opponentRange.label: the same range as the small-bet version, held fixed on purpose so that only the price changes

assumptions: The range is deliberately identical to the small-bet scenario so that the only thing that changes is the size of the bet. In real play a much larger bet usually means a narrower, stronger range, which would lower hero's equity further and make folding clearer still.
The price comparison assumes the hand reaches showdown with no further betting after the river card.
Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street; both players can cover this bet.
Only one card is left to come.
reasoning: Nothing about your hand has changed: same two hearts, same king-high board with no pair, same single card to come. What changed is the price, and the price is the decision. When a bet is larger than the pot, the share of the time you must end up best climbs a long way, and a one-card draw cannot climb with it. It is worth seeing how that requirement behaves as bets grow: it rises quickly through the small sizes, then more slowly, approaching but never passing even money no matter how enormous the bet gets. A draw that needed only a modest share against the small bet is now well short of what is required, so folding follows. The honest footnote is that holding the range fixed flatters your call here — an opponent who fires this much is usually doing it with a stronger set of hands than one who bets a token amount, which would only lower your equity. So the fold is safe in both directions: the price alone is enough to justify it, and the likely range shift points the same way.
commonMistakes: Reasoning that 'a draw is a draw' and calling any size with it. The hand is the same in both scenarios; the correct decision is opposite, and only the price moved.
Deciding the bet is 'too big to be strong' and calling to find out. That is a story about the opponent, not a price, and this range assumption gives it no support.
Calling because folding feels like being pushed off a hand. Folding to a large bet with a draw that is short of the required share is the arithmetic working, not a loss of nerve.

title: Where The Rule Of Four Drifts
question: Should hero call the all-in or fold?
facingAction: The big blind moves all in for 170 into a pot of 60.
assumptions: This is a face-up teaching spot: the opponent's hand is known, so the only uncertainty left is the two cards still to come. Being certain of an opponent's hand is the exception, not the normal case.
Calling puts the opponent all in, so both remaining cards will be dealt and no more units can go in. That is what makes a two-cards-to-come estimate the right kind of estimate here.
Neither of the opponent's cards is a heart, so none of hero's flush cards make the opponent a better hand.
Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street.
reasoning: The board is nine high with no pair, two hearts, and two connected cards, so your jack-ten of hearts has a flush draw and an open-ended straight draw at the same time. That large combined out count is exactly where the rule of 2 and 4 is least trustworthy, and it is worth being precise about why. The four-times version doubles the one-card estimate, which counts the runouts where you hit on both cards twice over, and the drift grows with the number of outs — so the biggest draws are where the shortcut flatters you most. It also assumes you get to see both cards for free, which is only true here because the bet puts all the units in now; with units left behind you might pay again on the turn or be priced out, and then the four-times figure is not the number you should be comparing at all. Work with the computed figure rather than the shortcut and the hand still holds up as a favourite against a pair of aces with no hearts, while the price on offer asks for clearly less than half. So calling follows. Two changes would flip it: if the opponent held a heart, part of your flush draw would be making you a losing hand rather than a winning one; and if the bet had left units behind, you would have to price the turn decision separately instead of buying both cards at once.
commonMistakes: Adding the flush outs to the straight outs without removing the cards that belong to both draws, then multiplying the inflated count by four.
Using the four-times estimate when the bet does not put you all in. With units behind, you are buying one card at a time and paying separately for the second.
Assuming any big draw is a favourite. Against a hand that shares your suit or blocks your straight card, the same shaped draw can be a clear underdog.
Treating the shortcut's answer as the answer. It is a table aid with a known direction of error, and the app will show you both figures side by side.

title: Gutshot Against A Pot-Sized Bet
question: Should hero call or fold?
facingAction: The button bets 90 into a pot of 90.

opponentRange.notation: QQ, 88, 55, 33, AQ, KQ, QJs, AJs, KJs, T9s, 76s, 65s, A5s, A4s
opponentRange.label: a turn betting range of top pair and better, a couple of small pairs, and some hands with nothing

assumptions: The button bets this turn with the range stated; a range containing fewer hands with nothing would make hero's equity lower still.
The price comparison assumes the hand reaches showdown with no further betting after the river card.
Every suit appears exactly once on this board, so no flush can be made by anyone — hero's two clubs are decoration, not a draw.
Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street.
reasoning: Start with the board: queen high, no pair, and all four suits present, which means no flush is possible for anybody on the river. With the queen and the eight out there, your jack-ten needs one specific rank — a nine — to make a straight, and that is the thinnest of the standard draws. A pot-sized bet is a useful landmark to hold in your head, because it is where the price stops being generous: you are being asked to risk the size of the pot to win it. As the bet grows relative to the pot, the share of the time you must be best grows too — fast through the small sizes, then more gently, approaching but never passing even money. A single-rank draw with one card to come is nowhere near that landmark, even after crediting the times a jack or a ten pairs and beats the hands in this range that have nothing. So this is a fold, and it is not close. What makes the spot worth studying is that the same hand against the same range becomes a reasonable call if this opponent bets a quarter of this amount instead: the cards did not change, the required share did. Get in the habit of pricing the bet before you evaluate the hand, because the bet is what sets the bar the hand has to clear.
commonMistakes: Calling because 'I have a draw' without asking what share of the time the draw needs to arrive at this particular price.
Assuming two suited cards in hand always add something. On a board showing all four suits, no flush can be made at all.

Believing a pot-sized bet needs about half the equity to call. The requirement is well below even money, and it stays below it however large the bet gets — which is why very large bets still cannot demand a coin flip.
Counting a pair of jacks or tens on the river as a win against every hand in the range, when most of the range already has this hand beaten.

title: Second Pair Against A Wide Range
question: Should hero call or fold?
facingAction: The big blind bets 60 into a pot of 100.

opponentRange.notation: AK, AQ, AJ, AT, A9s, A5s, A4s, KQ, KJ, QJ, JTs, T9s, 76s, 65s, KK, QQ, JJ, 77, 55, 44, 33, 22
opponentRange.label: a wide, aggressive turn barrelling range: every ace worth betting, the broadway cards, and small pairs

assumptions: This opponent bets the turn with the wide range stated. That is a read about a player, and the whole answer here depends on it.
The price comparison assumes the hand reaches showdown with no further betting after the river card.
All four suits are on the board, so no flush is possible for anyone, and no hand in the range assumed here can complete a straight with one card. Hands are therefore compared as pairs and high cards.
Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street.
reasoning: Read the board: ace high, no pair, and all four suits present, so no flush can be made by anybody, and nothing in the range assumed here can complete a straight with a single card. That strips the hand down to something simple — you hold second pair, which loses to any ace and beats most unpaired hands without one — though not all of them, since a hand like T9s pairs the same nine and outkicks you. With no flush or straight to worry about, your equity is close to a pure hand-reading question: what share of this opponent's betting range does not contain an ace, a bigger pair, or a card that pairs the board harder than you do? A small pair counts against you when its rank is on the board — 33 here is a set, not an underpair. Against a range this wide — one that keeps firing with broadway cards, small pairs and the odd hand with nothing — that share is large enough to clear the price being offered, so calling follows. Notice where the equity comes from: mostly from hands you already beat, not from improving, although a river nine or eight does promote you. The call is a consequence of the range, not of the hand: the same second pair at the same price is a fold against a narrow range, which is the companion scenario. If you think this particular opponent only bets the turn with an ace or better, then the assumption is what you should argue with, not the arithmetic that follows from it.
commonMistakes: Judging second pair by how it feels rather than by what it beats inside a stated range. The same hand can be a clear call or a clear fold at an identical price.
Assuming a bet on the turn means a strong hand. Against an opponent who bets often, most of the range is hands that have missed.
Looking for a draw to justify the call. No flush is available to anyone here and no straight to anything in this range, so the only question is whether you are ahead often enough.

title: Same Bet, Narrow Range, Different Answer
question: Should hero call or fold?
facingAction: The big blind bets 60 into a pot of 100.

opponentRange.notation: AA, KK, QQ, JJ, TT, AK, AQ, AJs, KQs
opponentRange.label: a narrow, value-heavy turn range: big pairs and big aces, with one suited hand that can be betting without a pair

assumptions: This opponent bets the turn only with the narrow range stated, and almost never without a pair or an ace. That is an assumption about a person, not a fact about poker.
The price comparison assumes the hand reaches showdown with no further betting after the river card.
All four suits are on the board, so no flush is possible for anyone, and no hand in this narrow range can complete a straight with one card. Hands are therefore compared as pairs and high cards.
Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street; the cards, the pot and the bet are identical to the wide-range scenario.
reasoning: Every visible fact is the same as in the wide-range version: same second pair, same ace-high board where no flush is possible and no hand in this range can make a straight, same pot, same bet, same price. The only thing that changed is who you have decided is betting. Against a range built from big pairs and big aces, second pair is behind nearly all of it, and the river cards that promote you to trips or two pair arrive too seldom to bridge the gap the price demands, so folding follows. This is the most useful thing to take from the pair of scenarios: an equity figure is not a property of your cards, it is a statement about your cards against an assumed range, and moving the assumption can reverse the decision without a single card changing. It also shows why 'am I getting the right price?' cannot be answered on its own. The price is fixed by the bet and the pot and is not open to argument; the equity is an estimate that inherits every weakness of your read. When those two are close, spend your thinking on the read rather than on recomputing the price.
commonMistakes: Remembering the answer from the wide-range version and applying it here. The visible situation is identical; only the range assumption differs, and it is the range that decides.
Calling to 'keep them honest' against an opponent you have already decided rarely bluffs. Those two beliefs contradict each other.
Treating the equity number the app shows as a fact about your hand rather than a consequence of the range you typed in.
Counting the river cards that improve you as if improving were the same as winning. Against this range some of those cards still leave you behind.

title: Drawing To A Second-Best Flush
question: Should hero call or fold?
facingAction: The button bets 55 into a pot of 70.
assumptions: This is a face-up teaching spot: the opponent's two diamonds are known. Away from a lesson you would have to estimate how often a range like theirs holds two of your suit.

The price comparison assumes the hand reaches showdown with no further betting after the river card. In practice the cards that complete hero's flush are also the cards hero pays off with, which makes calling worse than the immediate figure suggests.
Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street.
Only one card is left to come, so every out is a single-card out.
reasoning: Read the board before reading your hand: ace high, no pair, two diamonds, and with the four and the deuce out there your six-five also has a gap to fill, so it looks like a hand with two ways to win. The opponent's cards are face up here, and they rewrite the picture: they hold two higher diamonds, so every diamond that completes your flush completes a bigger one for them. Those cards are not outs — they are the most expensive cards in the deck for you, because they are precisely the ones that will make you happy to put units in. What is actually left is the cards that pair you and the cards that fill the gap, and here is the part worth remembering: the number of cards that genuinely rescue you is the same size as the flush draw you thought you had, and not one of them is a card you were counting. At this price you need a larger share than that count provides, so folding follows. The general lesson is that an out is only an out relative to the hand you are up against, and the outs that are easiest to count are the ones most likely to be shared.
commonMistakes: Counting a flush draw at full value without asking whether a bigger flush is possible for the hand you are facing.
Treating the extra straight card as a bonus on top of the flush draw, when against this opponent it is doing all of the work.
Calling because the hand has two ways to improve. Two ways to improve is not two ways to win if one of them makes a second-best hand.
Thinking of dominated draws as an unlucky accident. They are a predictable feature of drawing with low cards to a suit that bigger hands also want.

title: Big Favourite On A Connected Flop
question: Should hero call the all-in or fold?
facingAction: Hero checks and the button moves all in for 150 into a pot of 90.

opponentRange.notation: TT, 99, 77, 66, T9s, T9o, 98s, 65s, 54s, JJ, QQ, KK, AA, A5s, KQs, QJs, JTs
opponentRange.label: a short-stacked jamming range: some made straights, smaller sets, overpairs, and a lot of draws

assumptions: The button jams the range stated. It contains made straights as well as draws — if it were mostly straights the same call would be far closer.
Calling puts the opponent all in, so both remaining cards are dealt and no more units can go in.
Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street; the button has a short stack, which is why jamming is a normal choice for them.
The units in play are free practice units with no value, so the only thing at stake in a lost pot is what it teaches you.
reasoning: Read the board out loud: eight high, no pair, three cards in sequence and two hearts — one of the most connected flops there is. Your pair of eights has made three of a kind, and against the jamming range assumed here you are a clear favourite, so the price is met with a lot of room and calling follows. The interesting part is what 'favourite' does and does not mean. This texture already allows a made straight, and several hands that do not have one yet will finish with a straight or a flush, so a comfortable favourite here still loses the pot often enough that you will notice it. That is variance doing exactly what it is supposed to do: nothing about a run of lost pots means you played them wrong, and nothing about a lost pot makes the next one more likely to be yours. The practical care is in the planning rather than in this decision: on a board like this you can name in advance the cards that beat you, and if the units were not all in now you would want to think about how much you are willing to put in on later streets. Being a big favourite is a reason to get units in, not a reason to stop reading the board.
commonMistakes: Reading three of a kind as a hand that cannot lose. On three connected cards with two of a suit, plenty of runouts get there against you.
Folding a big favourite because the board looks frightening. The texture is a reason to expect to lose sometimes, not a reason to pass up a good price.
Interpreting a run of lost pots in spots like this as being 'due' for a win, or as evidence the call was wrong. Each hand is dealt from a fresh deck and the price was either good or it was not.
Assuming the jam is always a draw. This range contains hands that are already better than three of a kind, and that is what keeps the decision from being free.

title: Equity Against One Known Hand
question: Should hero call or fold?
facingAction: The button bets 75 into a pot of 150.
assumptions: This is a face-up teaching spot: the opponent's hand is known exactly, which is the least realistic assumption in this batch and the reason the number looks so comfortable.
The price comparison assumes the hand reaches showdown with no further betting after the river card.
All four suits are on the board, so no flush is possible for anyone, and neither of these two known hands can make a straight; the river only matters if it pairs a card in play.
Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street.
reasoning: The board is queen high, unpaired, and shows all four suits, so no flush is possible for anybody, and neither of these two hands can make a straight — the river only matters if it pairs a card in play. Both players hold a queen, so both have top pair, and the whole matchup comes down to the second card: yours is bigger. Against this one hand you are a large favourite, because the opponent needs their kicker rank to arrive on a single card, and calling is straightforward at this price. The number is not the lesson, though — where the number came from is. It answers a very narrow question: how do I do against exactly this hand? That question is answerable with certainty and almost never available at the table, because you can seldom see an opponent's cards. The companion scenario puts the identical hand at the identical price against the whole range that a hand like this belongs to, and the answer is much less comfortable. So whenever you see a large equity figure, check which question it answered: one hand you have convinced yourself of, or everything the opponent could be holding.
commonMistakes: Taking a hand-versus-hand figure as the equity for the decision. It is the equity against one holding you picked, and picking is where the error usually lives.
Assuming a shared top pair makes the pot close. With one card to come and a better kicker, the gap between the two hands is wide.
Forgetting that a kicker only decides the pot when the top card is shared; against a hand with a pair below yours the kicker is irrelevant.

title: Equity Against The Whole Range
question: Should hero call or fold?
facingAction: The button bets 75 into a pot of 150.

opponentRange.notation: AQ, KQ, QQ, QTs, Q9s, 99, 55, 33, JTs, T8s, 76s, 65s, A5s, KJs
opponentRange.label: a turn betting range: better kickers, two pair and sets, and a share of hands with nothing

assumptions: The button bets the turn with the range stated. Widen it towards hands with nothing and hero's equity rises; trim it towards the better queens and it falls.
The price comparison assumes the hand reaches showdown with no further betting after the river card.

All four suits are on the board, so no flush is possible for anyone; a couple of hands in this range can still complete a straight if the right river card arrives, which is part of why hero's figure here is lower than in the face-up version.
The cards, the pot and the bet are identical to the face-up scenario; only the knowledge of the opponent's hand has been removed.
reasoning: Identical cards, identical price, one change: you no longer get to see the opponent's hand. Now your top pair has to answer to everything that would bet this turn — the queens with a better second card, the two pairs and sets, and the hands with nothing at all. Averaged over that mixture you are still ahead often enough to beat the price, so calling still follows, but the roomy margin from the face-up version is gone. That is what an equity figure honestly is: an average over a range you assumed, which moves when the assumption moves. It is also worth noticing which hands sit where. The hands that beat you are the ones most likely to keep betting on the river, and the hands you beat are the ones most likely to give up, so an average in your favour is not the same as being comfortable about the rest of the hand. Use the range figure to make the decision and keep the hand-versus-hand figure for understanding a single matchup, never the other way round.
commonMistakes: Assuming your opponent holds the specific hand you can beat, computing against that, and calling on the strength of a number that answered the wrong question.
Swinging the other way and assuming the strongest hand in the range. Both errors come from replacing a range with a single hand.
Reading 'the average is in my favour' as 'this hand is easy'. The average includes many hands you crush and a few that have you dominated.
Forgetting that the two hole cards you hold remove combinations from the opponent's range, which is part of why the figures move.

title: Implied Odds With Deep Stacks
question: Should hero call or fold?
facingAction: The button bets 120 into a pot of 130.

opponentRange.notation: KK, JJ, 88, 22, AK, KQ, KJs, KTs, QJs, JTs, AJ, 98s
opponentRange.label: a value-heavy turn betting range built around the king and the jack

assumptions: The button bets the turn with the value-heavy range stated, and has enough behind to pay a river bet.
The immediate price comparison the app shows assumes no further betting. Implied odds are exactly the relaxation of that assumption, so the two figures are answering different questions.

Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street: far more is behind than is currently in the middle, which is what makes the later units worth counting.
Implied odds only count if the extra units actually arrive — the opponent must still be in the hand, still have units behind, and be willing to pay.
Hero's draw makes the best possible flush on this board, so the units won when it arrives are not at risk from a bigger flush.
reasoning: Board first: king high, no pair, two diamonds, and nothing in the range assumed here that can make a straight. Your ace-five of diamonds is drawing to the best flush this board can make, which matters because it means the units you win when the draw arrives are not going to a bigger version of your own hand. Now the price: the bet is close to the size of the pot with one card to come, and a single-card flush draw supplies less than that price demands, so on the immediate price alone this is a fold. What changes the conversation is the depth of the stacks. There is far more behind than there is in the middle, so the pot you are actually playing for is not the one you can see, and the units you expect to win on the river when a diamond lands are what has to cover the shortfall. That is what implied odds means, and it is an estimate about a person rather than a calculation about cards: against an opponent who pays off a river bet the call is defensible, and against one who shuts down the moment the flush card lands it is a straightforward fold. Two checks before you lean on it — be confident the hand you are drawing to will actually be best when it arrives, and be confident you will not be priced out by another large bet before you get there.
commonMistakes: Calling and calling it 'implied odds' without ever estimating how many units you expect to win later, or asking whether this opponent would pay them.
Applying implied odds to a draw that will not be best when it arrives. Extra units on later streets help most when the hand you make is the strongest one available.
Forgetting that the opponent has implied odds too: a deep stack behind you can also cost you units on the streets where you are the one who is beaten.
Treating the app's immediate price figure as the whole answer, when it is explicitly computed as though the betting stops here.

title: Weak Ace And Reverse Implied Odds
question: Should hero call this bet, and what is the plan for the river?
facingAction: The button bets 25 into a pot of 90.

opponentRange.notation: AK, AQ, AJ, AT, A9s, A8s, A5s, 99, 66, 22, KQs, KJs, QJs, JTs, T8s, 76s
opponentRange.label: a turn betting range of better aces, sets, and some hands with nothing

assumptions: The button bets the turn with the range stated, and will bet the river with the aces that have hero outkicked.
The immediate price comparison assumes no further betting. This scenario is about what happens when that assumption is false, so read the computed figure as the answer to a one-street question only.

All four suits are on the board, so no flush is possible for anyone; one suited hand in this range can complete a straight with the right river card, and otherwise the pot is decided by pairs and kickers.
Stacks shown are the units each player has left behind right now, after anything already committed on this street: enough behind for a river bet that dwarfs this one.
Hero's kicker is below the nine on the board, so almost every other ace in this range outkicks it; only the weakest ace listed does not.
reasoning: Read the board: ace high, no pair, all four suits present, so no flush is coming and, apart from one suited hand in this range that can fill a straight, the pot will be decided by pairs and kickers. You have top pair and the bet is tiny, so against the range assumed here the immediate arithmetic clears the bar easily — as a single-street question this is a call, and the app will show you that. Now look at what that figure quietly assumed: that the hand ends after the river with no more units going in. In this spot that is exactly what will not happen. Your kicker is the problem, because nearly every hand in this range that keeps betting the river either has you outkicked or has made three of a kind, while the hands you are beating are the ones that will give up and pay you nothing. That asymmetry is reverse implied odds: ahead you win a small pot, behind you lose a large one, and the units you will lose later are part of the price of calling now. The decision that follows is a call with a plan attached — you are calling one small bet and you are not calling a large river bet with this hand, and you are not raising it for value either. Against an opponent whose betting range is mostly better aces, folding now is better than calling twice, and if this same ace had a kicker that could win a big pot none of this would apply.
commonMistakes: Reading 'the immediate price is met' as 'calling is profitable'. The price is met for one street, and hands like this rarely get to stop after one street.
Valuing top pair by the rank of the pair while ignoring the kicker, on a board where the kicker is the only thing that can separate two aces.
Calling to 'see what the river brings' with a hand that cannot profitably call a river bet and cannot raise one either.
Confusing this with implied odds. Here the later units flow the other way, and the extra streets are a cost rather than a bonus.
